# The Internet Routing System and the Security Problem Space

The security problem is the size and the economics of one distributed table. This chapter fixes the objects every later control talks about: prefixes, origin ASes, paths, and the business relationship that decided the announcement was acceptable.

## Learning goals

- Read a global table entry as prefix, origin, path, and neighbour relationship
- Separate "how a packet is forwarded" from "who was allowed to announce the route"
- Name the 1990s design choices that left BGP without origin or path authentication
- Place a hijack, a leak, and an outage in that same table

## The Routing Table: Scale, Structure, and Daily Churn

A border router in the default-free zone holds on the order of a million IPv4 prefixes and a few hundred thousand IPv6 prefixes. Around 29 October 2026, public routing statistics put the combined announced prefix count near 1.5 million, with on the order of 120,000 autonomous systems visible. Those numbers drift every day. Use them for capacity planning, then measure your own routers.

Each selected route is a record with a destination prefix, a next hop, an AS path, and a set of attributes (origin code, MED, communities, and whatever local preference your policy wrote). The **origin AS** is the rightmost AS in the path as BGP sends it: the network that injected the prefix. The **neighbour** is the AS that handed the update to you, which is the leftmost hop from your point of view.

Churn is normal. De-aggregates appear for traffic engineering and for failures. A security system that pages on every new more-specific will train operators to ignore it. The useful signal is a more-specific or a new origin for a prefix you care about, or a path that violates a relationship you can check.

## How a Packet Travels: From Source to Destination Through Autonomous Systems

Forwarding uses the selected route's next hop. The AS path is not a source route. It is a loop-prevention record and a policy hint. Traffic enters your AS from a customer, a peer, or a transit provider, follows your interior forwarding toward the BGP next hop, and leaves toward whichever neighbour won the decision process.

Two facts fall out of that for security:

- You can attract traffic by announcing a prefix that other networks prefer, often a more-specific, without being anywhere near the legitimate destination.
- You can also accept a route you should not re-advertise, and then you become the network that carries someone else's traffic into the wrong place. That second failure is a **leak**. The announcement can be cryptographically valid at the origin and still be a policy violation.

Interior routing (OSPF, IS-IS, or iBGP with route reflectors) only moves the packet toward the selected BGP next hop inside your AS. Reflection and confederations change who inside the AS sees which exit. They do not add evidence about whether the exit was allowed to announce the prefix. **BGP Route Reflectors** covers the scaling mechanics.

## The Economic and Political Architecture of the Internet: Customers, Peers, and Transit Providers

Routing policy follows who pays whom.

| Relationship | Who announces what | Security default |
|--------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Customer | Their own prefixes and their customers' prefixes | Accept a known set. Tag it so you do not send it to other peers or transits except as your own customer cone |
| Peer (settlement-free) | Their own cone, not their transit providers' full table | Accept their cone. Do not accept the rest of the Internet from them |
| Transit provider | A full table, or a default, toward you | You accept broadly. You announce only your cone to them |

Gao–Rexford valley-free forwarding is the compact form of those contracts: a path goes up from customers toward providers, across at most one peering, then down toward customers. A route that goes down and then up again is the shape of a leak. ASPA later encodes the "up" direction as signed provider lists. Until that coverage is dense, the same shape has to be enforced with filters and with the Only-to-Customer attribute (RFC 9234) on sessions that speak it.

These relationships are contractual and often invisible in the protocol. Two networks can peer in one city and buy transit in another. Any filter generated from a single public guess of "who is a peer" will be wrong somewhere. Your authoritative source is your peering database, not a stranger's inference.

## Why BGP Inherently Lacks Security: Design Trade-offs of the 1990s

BGP-4 (RFC 4271) distributes reachability among networks that already decided to trust a TCP session. The designers optimised for policy and for partial information, which is what inter-domain routing requires, and they did not bind announcements to the holder of the address block. There is no signature on the origin. There is no signature on the path. Any neighbour can assert any prefix, any AS path, and most optional attributes.

That was a workable trade-off when the default-free zone was a small club of operators who could call each other. It is a poor fit for a table anyone can join by buying transit and bringing up one session. The controls in the rest of this part are additions around that core. They do not replace the decision process, and a router with no import policy still believes the session.

## Real-World Consequences: A Brief History of Major Routing Incidents

The same two shapes recur.

**Origin hijacks and more-specifics.** In February 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced YouTube's address space as a more-specific via PCCW. Networks that preferred the longer prefix sent users to Pakistan. YouTube recovered by announcing still longer prefixes, and PCCW then filtered the neighbour. The lesson that still holds: a more-specific beats a valid aggregate in the decision process, and the network that accepted the customer announcement exported the incident to everyone else.

**Leaks of an otherwise legitimate table.** Large providers have repeatedly re-advertised routes learned from one peer or transit toward another. The origins were real. The path was not a path the origin chose. Recipients who accepted a full table from a network that should only have sent a cone installed the leak. China Telecom's 2010 propagation of a large foreign table, and later leaks through well-connected regional providers, are this shape. Filtering on relationship beats origin validation here, because origin validation says Valid.

**Self-withdrawal.** In October 2021 Facebook removed its own routes from the Internet during an internal outage. That was not a hijack. Detection that only looks for a foreign origin misses an operator deleting themselves. Chapter 19 treats "our prefixes disappeared" as its own incident class.

**Collateral from a ROA mistake.** A holder that publishes a ROA and then announces a length or an origin the ROA does not cover becomes RPKI Invalid. Networks that drop Invalid stop reaching them. The security control worked. The outage is still yours if you cannot withdraw the ROA or fix the announcement quickly. Chapter 20 is that lifecycle.

## Summary

- The table is large, and ordinary churn hides careless alerts
- Forwarding follows the selected next hop; the AS path is evidence of policy, not a guarantee of the path taken
- Customer, peer, and transit are different acceptance problems
- BGP will carry any announcement a neighbour sends
- Hijacks, leaks, and self-inflicted ROA outages are different incidents and need different controls
